title: What English has to add
goal: Translate -mIş, -DIr and dropped pronouns into natural English, and choose the Turkish form for English hearsay and guesses.

intro.text: English has no evidential suffix, so `-mIş` becomes **apparently**, **must have**, **it turned out** or a surprised **you've…**, depending on its job; `-DIr` is **must** as a guess and nothing in a formal statement. And Turkish *o* makes English choose **he**, **she** or **they**.

vocab.en: apparently, by the look of it
according to legend, so the story goes
who knows (kim bilir ne zaman: who knows when)
to pass on, to convey; to render (in another language)

exercises.question: You see Ali's coat on the hook and say *Ali gelmiş!* Which English fits?
options: Ali came, apparently: someone told me.
Once upon a time Ali came.

why.1: Nobody told you: you are drawing a conclusion from the coat.
why.2: That is the `-mIş` of tales; here you are talking about now.
why.3: The pluperfect needs another past event to come before; it would be *gelmişti*.

exercises.explain: Inference from evidence: **must be here**, **looks like Ali's here**. The same *Ali gelmiş* after a phone call would be **Ali's here, apparently**.

accept: The neighbours have moved, apparently.
[Apparently|Reportedly] the [neighbours|neighbors] (have) moved (out|away)
[It seems|I hear|I heard|They say] (that) the [neighbours|neighbors] (have) moved (out|away)
The neighbours moved (out|away), [apparently|I hear|I heard|it seems|they say]
The neighbours have moved, I hear
The neighbours have moved, I heard
The neighbours have moved, it seems
The neighbours have moved, they say
The neighbours have moved out, [apparently|I hear|I heard|it seems|they say]
The neighbours have moved away, [apparently|I hear|I heard|it seems|they say]
The neighbors (have) moved (out|away), [apparently|I hear|I heard|it seems|they say]
The [neighbours|neighbors] seem to have moved (out|away)
It looks like the [neighbours|neighbors] (have) moved (out|away)

reject.why: Correct, but it loses `-mIş`: you didn't see it, someone told you. Add **apparently** or **I hear**.

exercises.hint: You weren't there: someone told you.
exercises.explain: Hearsay `-mIş` needs a word in English: **apparently**, **I hear**, **it seems**. Once is enough for a whole report.

exercises.task: Translate into natural English. Keep the narrator's distance from what she was told.
exercises.source: Meğer yeni komşu bir haftalığına tatile gitmiş, kediye de kapıcı bakıyormuş.
models: It turned out the new neighbour had gone away on holiday for a week, and the caretaker was looking after the cat.
Apparently the new neighbour was away for a week, and the caretaker had been feeding the cat.
checklist: *Meğer* comes out as **it turned out** or **apparently**
`-mIş` reads as hearsay or discovery, not as a plain past

exercises.en: Don't worry, they must have arrived long ago by now.

accept: varmışlardır

reject.why: *Varmışlar* passes on news. **Must have** is a confident guess: `-mIştIr`, *varmışlardır*.
*Vardılar* states a fact you know; the English is a guess: *varmışlardır*.

exercises.hint: Use *varmak*, as a confident guess about **they**.
exercises.explain: `-mIş` + `-lAr` + `-DIr`: the assumptive `-DIr` of [C1 unit 2](gp-dir-assumption), English **must have**.

accept: She must be tired; let's let her rest.
She must be tired, let her rest
She must be tired, let's leave her to rest
She must be tired, let's leave her alone to rest
She must be tired, let's let her get some rest
He must be tired, [let's let him rest|let him rest|let's leave him to rest|let's leave him alone to rest|let's let him get some rest]
They must be tired, [let's let them rest|let them rest|let's leave them to rest|let's let them get some rest]
She is probably tired, [let's let her rest|let her rest|let's leave her to rest]
He is probably tired, [let's let him rest|let him rest|let's leave him to rest]
exercises.explain: `-mIştIr` as a confident guess: **must be tired**. *O* has no gender, so **he**, **she** or **they** all fit until the context decides; keep the same one in both halves.

exercises.question: An encyclopedia says *Roman ilk kez 1900'de yayımlanmıştır.* Which English is right?
options: The novel was first published in 1900.
The novel must have been first published in 1900.
Apparently, the novel was first published in 1900.
The novel had been first published in 1900.

why.1: No guess here: encyclopedic `-mIştIr` states a fact ([C1 unit 2](gp-dir-general-truth)).
why.2: **Apparently** would add a doubt that the encyclopedia doesn't have.
why.3: The pluperfect needs an earlier past to refer to.

exercises.explain: In formal and reference style, `-DIr` adds authority, not doubt. English simply states the fact.

exercises.prompt: Apparently the museum is closed on Mondays.
accept: Müze pazartesi günleri kapalıymış.
Müze pazartesileri kapalıymış
[Pazartesileri|Pazartesi günleri] müze kapalıymış
[Görünüşe göre|Söylenene göre|Anlaşılan] müze [pazartesileri|pazartesi günleri] [kapalı|kapalıymış]
[Görünüşe göre|Söylenene göre|Anlaşılan] [pazartesileri|pazartesi günleri] müze [kapalı|kapalıymış]

reject.why: *Kapalıdır* states the rule, like a notice; **apparently** passes on what you heard: *kapalıymış*.

exercises.explain: Hearsay on a noun predicate is the copula `-(y)mIş`: *kapalıymış*. A word such as *görünüşe göre* can carry it instead.

accept: It turned out nobody had locked the door.
It turned out no one had locked the door
It turned out that [nobody|no one] had locked the door
[Nobody|No one] had locked the door, it turned out
As it turned out, [nobody|no one] had locked the door
It turns out (that) [nobody|no one] (had) locked the door
Turns out [nobody|no one] (had) locked the door
So [nobody|no one] had locked the door after all
exercises.explain: *Meğer* + `-mIş`: a discovery about what was true all along, **it turned out**. The English pluperfect places the locking before the discovery.

exercises.question: Which Turkish sentence keeps the genders of **She told him the truth**?

why.1: Correct Turkish, but **she** and **him** vanish: *ona* can be anyone.
why.3: **Him** is lost, and *kız* is a girl.

exercises.explain: Turkish pronouns have no gender. When it matters, Turkish names the people: *kadın*, *adam*.

exercises.tr: Söylenene göre yeni komşu çok iyi biriymiş.
exercises.en: Reportedly, the new neighbour is a very nice person.
